newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian farm incomes fall in 1996/97 - ABARE.
newsitem.headline: Australian farm incomes fall in 1996/97 - ABARE.

text.p: Lower prices for major Australian rural commodities resulted in reduced average farm cash incomes in most industries surveyed in 1996/97 ending June 30, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said on Thursday.

The fall in income was estimated to have been greatest for specialist grain producers, with incomes falling sharply from the very high levels of 1995/96, ABARE's acting executive director Stephen Beare said in a statement.
Beare said this while releasing ABARE's 1997 Australian Farm Surveys Report, which showed that average farm cash income in 1996/97 fell to an estimated A$47,100 from A$50,520 the year before.
The figure measures total receipts less cash costs.
Average cash income for specialist grain producers fell to A$112,000 from A$154,000 in the latest year,
Incomes of wool producing farms were estimated to have risen to A$10,700 in 1996/97 from the record low base of A$3,000 the year before.

This followed some reduction in farm costs, largely because of removal of a levy on wool production, but was combined with increased sale of wool from grower-held stocks which offset the impact of a decline in wool production and prices, Beare said.
Beef, however, did not fare as well, with lower prices reducing profits in some areas, he said.
Average beef income fell to A$10,800, the lowest level in about 20 years, from A$15,600.
"Lower cattle prices in 1996/97 have resulted in a further decline in profitability for a significant number of beef producers.
However, incomes for beef industry properties in regions in which the live cattle trade has been most prevalent are estimated to have remained largely unchanged," Beare said.
Marked differences occurred in financial performance among the broadacre industries.
Incomes for the mixed livestock-crops industry improved significantly because of a substantial increase in the area planted to crops and higher wool receipts offsetting lower grain prices, he said.
